Have received some prereading for tmrs meeting (in person). Its short but gives bare bone basics (Turci, n.d.).


The bare bones intro states: “This project will investigate how different operational definitions of quantum Markovianity appear in a single impurity model coupled to a structured environment.”
The project sketch outlines first steps:



simulate a “single impurity” directly
take a “fermionic system” w/single site coupled to a bath. This setup involves a single system site coupled to a bunch of bath sites. The combined system hamiltonian follows:

\(\hat{H}=\epsilon \hat{s}^{\dagger} \hat{s}+
\sum_{k=1}^N g_k(\hat{b}_k^{\dagger} \hat{s}+\hat{s}^{\dagger} \hat{b}_k)
+\sum_{k=1}^N \omega_k \hat{b}_k^{\dagger} \hat{b}_k.\)
The first term is the “on site” energy, the second is the system/bath coupling energy (hopping energy?), with the last term being the bath’s free energy. All these terms are described in terms of the systems and baths creation/annihalation operators (\(\hat{s}\) and \(\hat{b}\) respectively). There’s also some relation between the coupling \(g_{k}\) and the “spectral density”. Also also since only creation/annhilation operators are involved; can consider the hamiltonian non interaction (from reading around topic this prob relates to interaction picture; which is nice that i wont need to deal with that atm (i think interpreation is that bath sites don’t really interact with each other; and system site (of which there is only 1) doesnt interact with other system sites (because only 1)).
Fermionic anticommutation relations apply; determine stats.
The “all bath sites” connect to the single system site is called a “star geometry”.
Direct diagonalisation and time evolution evaluation of this system doesn’t scale well w/bath size; so isn’t useful for examining continuum limit (Note; if its quick, may still be worth implementing a solver for this; firstly as an exercise to familiarise myself w/problem setup, and to directly illustrate these scaling challenges).



Given non interacting hamiltonian; correlation matrix of system determines dynamics. Given an “operator vector”:
\(\hat{\mathbf{A}} = (\hat{s}, \hat{b}_1, \hat{b}_2, ..., \hat{b}_N)^T\)
Correlation matrix follows:
\(\mathbf{C}_{ij} = \langle \hat{A}_j^\dagger \hat{A}_i \rangle\)
These relate to the hamiltonian via a “single particle hamiltonian” \(h\) (unsure exactly what this represents):
\(\hat{H}=\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{\dagger} \mathbf{h} \hat{\mathbf{A}}=\sum_{i, j=1}^{\infty} h_{i j} \hat{A}_i^{\dagger} \hat{A}_j\)
The correlation matrix evolves as:
\(\mathbf{C}(t) = \mathbf{u}(t) \mathbf{C}(0) \mathbf{u}(t)^{\dagger}\) \(\mathbf{u}(t) = e^{-i \mathbf{h} t}\)
Since the system is what is of interest, and the first term in the operator vector \(\hat{A}\) represents the system; the reduced density operator for the system only requires the first term in the correlation matrix as:
\(\rho_S(t)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
1-\mathbf{C}_{11}(t) & 0 \\
0 & \mathbf{C}_{11}(t)
\end{array}\right)\)
I suspect in practice, the starting system state would inform \(C_{11}=\langle \hat{s}^{}\hat{s} \rangle\), and time evolution on \(C_{11}\) would be performed using the system single particle hamiltonian; then the reduced density operator can be computed for any time and examined. The specifics of how this is to be done are unclear to me atm.



Chain mapping maps system from “star geometry” to “semi-infinite” 1D chain. proceeds as: * discretize bath spectral density to determine bath couplings/modes * unitary transform maps bath onto 1D chain with nearest neighbour couplings (seemingly trying to “match” modes of complete bath?) - system couples at start of chain * resulting hamiltonian is seemingly nicely behaved and easy to simulate? * Note finite length of chain can cause “reflections” which can mess w/signal - there are ways to deal w/this



Key point of these sims is to extract “dynamical map” \(\Gamma\) which maps the initial reduced density \(\rho_{s}(0)\) to \(\rho_{s}(t)\) as \(\rho_{s}(t) = \Gamma(t, 0)\rho_{s}(0)\). This dynamical map becomes main “result” of simulations and is necessary for analysis.



The dynamical map can then be examined to test for memory effects using various different metrics:

memory kernels - defined by “Nakajima-Zwanzig formalism”
Information backflow - defined by BPL (Breuer-Laine-Piilo) measure
Failure of Completely positive (CP) divisibility - RHP (Rivas-Huelga-Plenio) measure

I’m unsure exactly what these different measures capture, but seem to be main “probes” into the system’s memory effects.

title: Dissertation information:
text:
Dissertation information:
Supervisor: Dr Francesco Turci  Co-supervisor: Prof Stephen Clark
Co-supervisor: Dr David Strachan
Lab partner: Hannah Sobieralska (initially, she’s had to take a year out for personal reasons, so am doing this project alone)
Project: Driving non-markovianity in open systems
Code: TP-M09



Project description:
An open system exchanges matter and energy with the environment. Typically, one distinguishes the system from the environment by separating scales: in space, the system is much smaller than the environment, and in time, the environment relaxes much more quickly than the system (it Markovian, i.e. memoryless). The two are, however, always coupled, with interfaces whose contributions are normally taken to be small. However, in open quantum systems, a clear separation between the system and the environment becomes more challenging, both conceptually and practically. Conceptually, the coupling between the system and the bath may be strong enough to lead to important memory effects, where the evolution of the system is strongly correlated in time, and the environment itself behaves differently from a purely thermalised state; from the practical point of view, computer modelling of open systems typically requires explicitly modelling both, i.e. simulating a closed system and examining two subsystems (the original system of interest and the remainder, intrepreted as the environment) (Heinz-Peter Breuer, and Francesco Petruccione 2007). In this project, we will investigate how such memory effects develop in computational models of open quantum systems, exploiting the Matrix Product State (MPS) formalism and tensor network methods (Brenes et al. 2020). We will explore how different models of system-bath coupling and structures affect the development of non-Markovian correlations both in the system and in the environment (DavidMpemba2025?). We will start by considering equilibration towards the thermal state and then focus on periodically driven couplings, which introduce additional timescales and allow us to observe the system stroboscopically (Floquet setting). This will take us to tackle situations in which dissipation coupled to periodic driving can lead to the emergence of non-trivial states, such as time crystals. You will build your project on in-house code in the dedicated, high-performance, scientific programming language Julia, along with existing advanced packages for the simulation of open quantum systems using tensor networks (ITensors). You will have the opportunity to explore both analytically tractable toy models and more complex simulation settings. You will have the opportunity to work on this frontier topic with support from David Strachan, a recently appointed EPSRC Postdoctoral Pathway Fellow working in this area. For further discussion of the project scope, please contact the project supervisor.





References

Brenes, Marlon, Juan José Mendoza-Arenas, Archak Purkayastha, Mark T. Mitchison, Stephen R. Clark, and John Goold. 2020. “Tensor-Network Method to Simulate Strongly Interacting Quantum Thermal Machines.” Physical Review X 10 (3): 031040. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevX.10.031040.


Heinz-Peter Breuer, and Francesco Petruccione. 2007. The Theory of Open Quantum Systems. https://doi.org/https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199213900.001.0001.

text:
Recaping to date, I have:

Set up labbook
Set up code repository locally
Received code and basic introduction from Dr Turci
Partly read introductory papers/books on the topic

Looking forwards, there are 2 more immediate things i need to do:

continue reading to build up understanding:

Second quantisation (Altland and Simons 2010)
Introductory paper (Rivas and Huelga 2012)

Build up main “computational engine”:

Look through and understand code Dr Turci has sent me
Refactor said code into a convenient utility I can use throughout this project


After i’ve done these i’ll be equiped with the main theoretical and computational tools for this project. This will inform the rest of the investigation of this project.
Having a practical understanding of what this project entails should help me understand the theory “in context”. As such, i think for now its worth examining the code Dr Turci has sent me, in order to start planning the computational engine.
Examining the provided julia code (Y4DissertationCodeMaterials/providedCode/basic-1site-bath-julia.ipynb), it starts by reiterating the maths. Note; explanation recommends finding a good explanation for “wick’s theorem”. Examining my old personal notes for QFT, i recall it being relevant to evaluating the non commuting terms in the Dyson series. That understanding was based on (Schwichtenberg 2020) which may be of use. However i wonder if the second quantisation (Altland and Simons 2010) chapter will introduce it in a more contextually relevant manner. Skimming the chapter it seems so… Changed my mind, i’m going to try and quickly skim the chapter with the remainder of this afternoon. I expect the concepts will be familiar, so shouldn’t take too long. Code examination can come tmr.


Second quantisation seems to be general framework of ladder operators and associated commutation relations; which is a familiar concept. Apparently generalises nicely to N-body quantum physics.
Chapter motivates second quantisation by highlighting computational issues w/many body QM due to indistinguishablity, symmetrization.antisymmetrization, and the exchange of particle numbers.


It then covers the “apparatus of second quantization”.
Compares representation of labelling particles in state individually to simply counting the number of particles in each state (I.E \(\ket{1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3}\) becomes \(\ket{4, 2, 1}\)). This is the “occuptation number representation”. Also note the “Fock space” \(\mathcal{F}\); made up of basis states \(\{ \ket{n_{i}} \}\) w/out occupation num condition \(\sum n_i = N\). Therefore many body state can be represented as \(\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{n_{i}} c_{n_i}\ket{n_{i}}\).
Within this framework, ladder operators can be constructed to act on \(\mathcal{F}\):
\(a_{i}^{\dagger}\ket{n_{1},...,n_{i},...}=(n_{i}+1)^{1/2}\zeta^{s_{i}}\ket{n_{1},...n_{i}+1,...}\) \(s_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}n_{j}\)
Note that in the fermionic case, the \(n_{i}+1\) operation is a mod 2 operation \(n_{i}+1 \equiv (n_{i}+1)\%2\) Utility of this; can generate all states by repeated application of \(a_{i}^{\dagger}\) to vacuum state:
\(\ket{n_{1},...}=\prod_{i}\frac{1}{(n_{i}!)^{1/2}}(a_{i}^{\dagger})^{n_{i}\ket{0}}\)


Wierd notation used by chapter for commutation/anti-commutation relations:
\([A,B]_{\zeta}=AB-\zeta AB\)
\([A,B]_{\zeta=+1}=[A,B]_{+}=AB-AB\) // commutator
\([A,B]_{\zeta=-1}=[A,B]_{-}=AB+AB=\{A,B\}\) // anticomutator
Note that:
\([a_i,a_j^{\dagger}]_{\zeta}=\delta_{ij}\)
\([a_i,a_j]_{\zeta}=0\)
\([a_i^{\dagger},a_j^{\dagger}]_{\zeta}=0\)



The chapter continues into the “practical aspects” of this framework.






NoteSingle particle base transforms



Firstly; switching between single particle bases \(\{ \lambda \} \to \{ \widetilde{\lambda} \}\) - the operators transform as:
\(a_{\widetilde{\lambda}}^{\dagger} = \sum_{\lambda}\braket{\lambda|\widetilde{\lambda}}a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}\)
\(a_{\widetilde{\lambda}} = \sum_{\lambda}\braket{\widetilde{\lambda}|\lambda}a_{\lambda}\)
where \(\lambda\) represents a particular particle state in a particular single particle basis. For continuous quantum numbers (I.E, pos) the sum becomes integrals as:
\(a_{\lambda}=\int_{0}^{L}dx\braket{\lambda|x}a(x)\)
\(a(x)=\sum_{k}\braket{x|\lambda}a_{\lambda}\)








NoteSingle particle operators



Secondly operators acting on single particles w/single party operator \(o_{n}\) on nth particle typically become \(\mathcal{O_{1}}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}o_{n}\).
Typical example noted is momentum: \(T=\sum_{n}\frac{p_{n}^2}{2m}\)
Also introduces “occupation number operator” which counts #particles in state:
\(n_{\lambda}=a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}a_{\lambda}\)
Which is useful for actually constructing \(\mathcal{O_{1}}\). Given \(o=\sum_{i}o_{\lambda_i}\ket{\lambda_i}\bra{\lambda_i}\), \(o_{\lambda_i}=\braket{\lambda_i | o | \lambda_i}\). Skipping over details i’m uninterested in rn, the general result is:
\(\mathcal{O_1}=\sum_{\mu\nu}\braket{\mu |o|\nu}a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}a_{\lambda}\)


The chapter then goes into concrete examples to cement these ideas - not immediately relevant, but earmarking p48 in case useful for later.



There’s also a practical applications section. Not going to go into that in depth; skimming to try to earmark anything of use:

Electrons in a periodic potential (goes through nearly free electrons -> tight binding)(p51)
Mott-hubbard transition and the magnetic state (p61)
interacting fermions in one dimension (p67)

this section starts using ideas of interaction vs non interacting terms - i suspect wicks theorem (and other useful bits) may be here

Quantum spin chains (76)
Summary and outlook - Ch summary (p83)

Wick theorem is not in this section - its mentioned in the summary. ctrl+f through the book doesn’t seem to have a contained explanation albeit many uses of Wick’s theorem. In which case (Schwichtenberg 2020) may be a better call - the mathematical machinery seems to generalize beyond QFT, so it should be applicable. Ctrl+f through (Schwichtenberg 2020), the explanation of contractions/Wick’s theorem goes between p426-p428 at minimum (more after that). Not a today thing to look at but worth earmarking for later.
This reading was a useful refresher and “earmarking exploration” - i think tmr i can go through the code in depth to understand what its doing/how its structured. I should be able to come up with a near term plan thereafter (wether i can get on w/the computational engine or if i need more reading).

Second quantisation seems to be general framework of ladder operators and associated commutation relations; which is a familiar concept. Apparently generalises nicely to N-body quantum physics.
Chapter motivates second quantisation by highlighting computational issues w/many body QM due to indistinguishablity, symmetrization.antisymmetrization, and the exchange of particle numbers.


It then covers the “apparatus of second quantization”.
Compares representation of labelling particles in state individually to simply counting the number of particles in each state (I.E \(\ket{1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3}\) becomes \(\ket{4, 2, 1}\)). This is the “occuptation number representation”. Also note the “Fock space” \(\mathcal{F}\); made up of basis states \(\{ \ket{n_{i}} \}\) w/out occupation num condition \(\sum n_i = N\). Therefore many body state can be represented as \(\ket{\Psi}=\sum_{n_{i}} c_{n_i}\ket{n_{i}}\).
Within this framework, ladder operators can be constructed to act on \(\mathcal{F}\):
\(a_{i}^{\dagger}\ket{n_{1},...,n_{i},...}=(n_{i}+1)^{1/2}\zeta^{s_{i}}\ket{n_{1},...n_{i}+1,...}\) \(s_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}n_{j}\)
Note that in the fermionic case, the \(n_{i}+1\) operation is a mod 2 operation \(n_{i}+1 \equiv (n_{i}+1)\%2\) Utility of this; can generate all states by repeated application of \(a_{i}^{\dagger}\) to vacuum state:
\(\ket{n_{1},...}=\prod_{i}\frac{1}{(n_{i}!)^{1/2}}(a_{i}^{\dagger})^{n_{i}\ket{0}}\)


Wierd notation used by chapter for commutation/anti-commutation relations:
\([A,B]_{\zeta}=AB-\zeta AB\)
\([A,B]_{\zeta=+1}=[A,B]_{+}=AB-AB\) // commutator
\([A,B]_{\zeta=-1}=[A,B]_{-}=AB+AB=\{A,B\}\) // anticomutator
Note that:
\([a_i,a_j^{\dagger}]_{\zeta}=\delta_{ij}\)
\([a_i,a_j]_{\zeta}=0\)
\([a_i^{\dagger},a_j^{\dagger}]_{\zeta}=0\)



The chapter continues into the “practical aspects” of this framework.






NoteSingle particle base transforms



Firstly; switching between single particle bases \(\{ \lambda \} \to \{ \widetilde{\lambda} \}\) - the operators transform as:
\(a_{\widetilde{\lambda}}^{\dagger} = \sum_{\lambda}\braket{\lambda|\widetilde{\lambda}}a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}\)
\(a_{\widetilde{\lambda}} = \sum_{\lambda}\braket{\widetilde{\lambda}|\lambda}a_{\lambda}\)
where \(\lambda\) represents a particular particle state in a particular single particle basis. For continuous quantum numbers (I.E, pos) the sum becomes integrals as:
\(a_{\lambda}=\int_{0}^{L}dx\braket{\lambda|x}a(x)\)
\(a(x)=\sum_{k}\braket{x|\lambda}a_{\lambda}\)








NoteSingle particle operators



Secondly operators acting on single particles w/single party operator \(o_{n}\) on nth particle typically become \(\mathcal{O_{1}}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}o_{n}\).
Typical example noted is momentum: \(T=\sum_{n}\frac{p_{n}^2}{2m}\)
Also introduces “occupation number operator” which counts #particles in state:
\(n_{\lambda}=a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}a_{\lambda}\)
Which is useful for actually constructing \(\mathcal{O_{1}}\). Given \(o=\sum_{i}o_{\lambda_i}\ket{\lambda_i}\bra{\lambda_i}\), \(o_{\lambda_i}=\braket{\lambda_i | o | \lambda_i}\). Skipping over details i’m uninterested in rn, the general result is:
\(\mathcal{O_1}=\sum_{\mu\nu}\braket{\mu |o|\nu}a_{\lambda}^{\dagger}a_{\lambda}\)


The chapter then goes into concrete examples to cement these ideas - not immediately relevant, but earmarking p48 in case useful for later.



There’s also a practical applications section. Not going to go into that in depth; skimming to try to earmark anything of use:

Electrons in a periodic potential (goes through nearly free electrons -> tight binding)(p51)
Mott-hubbard transition and the magnetic state (p61)
interacting fermions in one dimension (p67)

this section starts using ideas of interaction vs non interacting terms - i suspect wicks theorem (and other useful bits) may be here

Quantum spin chains (76)
Summary and outlook - Ch summary (p83)

Wick theorem is not in this section - its mentioned in the summary. ctrl+f through the book doesn’t seem to have a contained explanation albeit many uses of Wick’s theorem. In which case (Schwichtenberg 2020) may be a better call - the mathematical machinery seems to generalize beyond QFT, so it should be applicable. Ctrl+f through (Schwichtenberg 2020), the explanation of contractions/Wick’s theorem goes between p426-p428 at minimum (more after that). Not a today thing to look at but worth earmarking for later.
This reading was a useful refresher and “earmarking exploration” - i think tmr i can go through the code in depth to understand what its doing/how its structured. I should be able to come up with a near term plan thereafter (wether i can get on w/the computational engine or if i need more reading).
